Your reports agree with the register on most points. The exception is the ModelDuck literature review's top advice: it says to build three things first, and I deferred all three with a stock "revisit later" reason, without weighing the evidence the reports collected. I haven't changed anything yet.

The reports are in `reports/`: the ModelDuck literature review and its idea briefs, a "what ModelDuck can borrow from neurocore" report, and a research-engine report. Together with the notes in `research_notes/`, they're about 350 KB. Neither folder is tracked by git yet.

**What the reports say to build first, compared with the code today:**

| Report's priority | In the register | What the code does now |
|---|---|---|
| **#1: log every test item, with proper statistics** | 1037, deferred | The benchmark fails a run if the overall score drops by more than 0.01 points ([benchmarks/run.mjs:679](projects/modelduck/benchmarks/run.mjs#L679)). It covers about 14 prompts, with no per-item comparison and no confidence interval. So a single flipped check fails the gate, and a pass doesn't prove there was no regression. |
| **#2: check whether a model fits in memory, and refuse if not** | 903, approved but narrowed to "tell the user" | The engine quietly retries at smaller context sizes. The report wants a memory-fit card plus a refusal. |
| **#3: reuse the prompt and its cache between turns** | 873, deferred | Chat sessions are now reused (`a56065e`). But the default "Context overflow: shift" discards that cache, which the report names as the cost. |

**Where the reports already shaped what we did:**

| Report advice | Status |
|---|---|
| Lock the local API down (literature idea 4) | Done today as 1054 |
| Fingerprint every generation (neurocore report, tier 1) | The other agent built it; 1000 is rejected as already done |
| Default to a 4K context, with 8-bit KV in the Balanced preset; reject 32K (idea 14) | The code already matches |
| Don't add autonomous agents (15), small-model draft decoding (13) or Medusa-style multi-token decoding | Rejected or deferred, as the reports advise |
| The fast "n-gram" decoding, retrieval and memory prototypes (9–11) | Deferred, which fits the reports' "prototype with a clear stop condition" |

**What the reports flag that I missed:**
- **The "Token saver" preset still uses the 4-bit KV cache** ([src/config.js:61](projects/modelduck/src/config.js#L61)). Both the literature and ModelDuck's own baseline show a large quality drop with it. The preset only carries a warning, and the report recommends 8-bit instead. Changing it would need a benchmark run.
- **Undisclosed network use (idea 5, "honest egress ledger").** ModelDuck calls `getLlama()` with no build option, so node-llama-cpp defaults to building from source when no prebuilt binary fits ([src/engine.js:181](projects/modelduck/src/engine.js#L181)). That build would download llama.cpp from GitHub, which an "offline, no telemetry" app should never do silently. This comes from the library's documentation; I haven't triggered it.
- **Research-engine report:** it recommends tier 1 items 971–976 next. I approved 974 and 975 but deferred 971, 972, 973 and 976. It also says that project's test suite was failing because of a README length limit. Another agent is working there, so I haven't checked whether that's still true.

**What I'd change in the register:**
- **1037 (per-item benchmark statistics) → approve, P2.** The report ranks it #1, and the code confirms the gate is a raw threshold.
- **903 → widen** to the full memory-fit check that refuses to load, per the report.
- **New idea, P2:** set `build: "never"` (or ask first) so loading a model can never silently download and compile code.
- **New idea, P3:** switch the Token saver preset from 4-bit to 8-bit KV cache, gated on a benchmark run.
- **Keep 873 deferred,** with a note that it's the report's #3 and depends on the shift setting.
- **Research-engine 971–976:** re-review them against the report once that project's in-progress task is finished.

Should I apply these register changes? Separately, I'd also recommend committing `reports/` and `research_notes/` so the research isn't lost. Today they exist only as untracked files.

### 2. Versioned prompt and preset library with benchmark-gated trust
**What NeuroCore does.** `SkillVersionStore` stores every content change under its SHA-256,
keeps a bounded 50-version index per skill, and writes a rollback as a new version so the
rollback itself is auditable (`modules/skills/versions.py:1-149`). Promotion of an improvement
requires a perfect same-flow baseline with provenance, a perfect candidate and no regression;
the promoted version is recorded and can be rolled back (`modules/brain/improvement.py:279-376`).
**Why it fits ModelDuck.** The three presets are hardcoded and the README says they "fill the
settings form, never apply themselves, and only earn trust after both phases pass"
(`README.md:120-121`). Nothing records that a preset actually passed, and a user cannot save a
good system prompt at all. A versioned library turns the claim into state that can be inspected.
**What to add.**
- `prompts.json` and `presets.json` under `--home`, written through the existing atomic helper
  (`src/fs-atomic.js`) with quarantine on corruption.
- A version record: `{ n, sha256, createdAt, author, note, benchmarkRunUid, suiteVersion, testHash,
  promptFingerprint }`. Keep at most 50; prune oldest; never prune the active version. Rollback
  copies an old body into a new version.
- Trust state: `candidate` → `trusted` only when a run UID exists and its `suiteVersion`,
  `testHash` and `promptFingerprint` still match the current preset content. Any edit or
  prompt-affecting setting change resets it to `candidate`.
- Built-in presets stay immutable; "Clone" creates a user preset. A trusted preset only fills
  the settings form — it never applies itself.
- UI: list, diff, rollback, "Benchmark this preset" (runs both phases or attaches an existing
  run), "Use".
- Tests: pruning, rollback-as-new-version, trust invalidation on edit, refusal to trust without
  a run, stable ordering.
**Effort:** S–M (2–3 days). **Impact:** high for the benchmark moat and onboarding.
**Benchmark:** no generation change; if a default preset changes, run the gate. **Risk:** keep
the JSON human-readable; no database.
---
### 3. Pre-flight load plan with blocking and warning findings
**What NeuroCore does.** `simulate_flow` analyses structure, effects and a cost envelope without
executing a node. It returns `{ blocking, findings:[{severity, code, message, node_id, fix}],
cost, effects, cycles }`. A single pass that cannot fit is blocking; a cycle that *may* reach
the cap is a warning (`core/flow_simulation.py:1-321`, especially `290-320`). The editor and the
improvement engine gate on `blocking`, not on a score.
**Why it fits ModelDuck.** `engine.load` silently retries `[wanted, min(wanted, 3072), 2048, 1024]`
(`src/engine.js:257-287`) and only surfaces a generic OOM (`engine.js:59-75`). The user never
sees which context was planned, which fallback succeeded, or why. The GitHub research already
asks for a fit report (item 3); NeuroCore supplies the deterministic report shape.
**What to add.**
- `src/load-plan.js`, a pure function `planLoad({ entry, settings, system })` returning:
  - `blocking`: file missing or unreadable, incomplete shard set (`*-00001-of-0000N.gguf` with
    missing parts), bad GGUF magic, not enough disk for the model, requested context impossible
    at the smallest fallback.
  - `warning`: requested context above the trained context, `kvCache` `q4_0`/`q8_0` without
    flash attention (the engine forces it, so an info), GPU layers > 0 with the CPU backend,
    `mmap off` with a large model and low RAM, `sequences > 1` with a single context, an
    `mmproj-*.gguf` file selected directly, missing chat template, `maxTokens` close to the
    context, recent load failures with these settings.
  - `info`: effective context after fallback, estimated KV bytes, recommended threads, model
    size/quant.
- `GET /api/models/:id/plan?context=&kv=&backend=` returns the report without loading. The UI
  shows a "Load plan" drawer; warnings have "Load anyway". Record which fallback context
  actually succeeded in the response.
- Return the same report from a failed `POST /api/models/:id/load` instead of only the generic
  error.
- After `matrix-server-v2` lands, reuse the shape for `bench:model --plan`: number of variants,
  downloads, estimated time from history, variants likely to fail. A single pass that cannot
  fit is blocking; a matrix that may exceed a time budget is a warning.
**Effort:** S–M (2–3 days). **Impact:** medium-high — fewer support tickets and a stronger
"inspectable" story. **Benchmark:** no generation change; if the plan changes the default
context selection, run the gate. **Risk:** memory estimates are guesses; label them and never
block a user who accepts a warning. Only impossible states are blocking.
---
### 4. Per-request budget and JIT load budget
**What NeuroCore does.** `ExecutionBudget` bounds nodes, LLM calls, tokens, tool calls and wall
time. One budget is created per top-level run and shared by nested runs; flow metadata may
lower a limit but never raise it. `spend` raises `BudgetExceeded` with a why/fix; `pressure`
is a 0–1 signal; `snapshot()` is JSON-safe (`core/execution_budget.py:1-161`). `SelfBudget`
reserves a unit before the work starts and resets at UTC midnight
(`modules/brain/self_budget.py:1-154`).
**Why it fits ModelDuck.** ModelDuck runs one generation at a time by design. `maxTokens` bounds
the output, but nothing bounds prompt processing or wall time, and nothing prevents an API
client from forcing repeated JIT loads of different models (`src/jit.js:34-95`). A LAN client
can monopolize the single context.
**What to add.**
- `src/budget.js`: `createBudget({ maxPromptTokens, maxOutputTokens, maxSeconds,
  maxJitLoadsPerHour })` with `spend`, `checkTime`, `pressure`, `snapshot`.
- Per request: request `max_tokens`/`max_completion_tokens` may only lower `maxOutputTokens`;
  check `promptTokens + maxTokens <= context` (already in `engine.js:429-439`); a timer aborts
  with `budget_exceeded` and a why/fix. Add `budget` to `stats` and `/api/status`.
- JIT: a persisted `jit-loads.json` ledger counts loads in a rolling hour. `JitManager.ensure`
  reserves before loading and releases on failure; a denied reservation returns 429 with
  `Retry-After`. Add `maxJitLoadsPerHour` (default 6) to server settings.
- Tests: fake clock, lower-only override, wall-time abort, pressure snapshot, ledger reset,
  release on failed load.
**Effort:** S–M (2 days). **Impact:** medium — robustness for LAN/API use. **Benchmark:** no
quality change; the wall-time cap only affects runaway requests. **Risk:** keep default
`maxSeconds` generous (600) so normal long prompts are unaffected; make it configurable.
---

38	## Quantization is an artifact, not a label
39	
40	Only one quantization family executes natively in GGUF on CPU. GPTQ uses second-order layer-wise reconstruction; AWQ protects activation-salient weights with per-channel scaling; SmoothQuant migrates activation outliers for W8A8; LLM.int8() keeps outlier dimensions in FP16; QLoRA's NF4 is a training format (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2023; Dettmers et al., 2022; Dettmers et al., 2023). Their quality numbers do not transfer to a `.gguf` file because the artifacts are produced by different algorithms and executed by different kernels. GGUF K-quants are data-free block quantization with a 256-weight super-block split into eight sub-blocks of 32, plus quantized 6-bit scales and mins.
41	
42	The 8B evidence is the best-controlled GGUF data available. On WikiText-2, F16 perplexity is 6.2332; Q8_0 is 6.2343 (+0.04%, KLD 0.0014, RMS Δp 1.20%); Q6_K is 6.2534 (+0.32%, KLD 0.0055); Q5_K_M is 6.2886 (+0.89%, KLD 0.0108, RMS 3.16%); Q4_K_M is 6.4071 (+2.8%, KLD 0.0313, RMS **5.52%**); Q4_0 is 6.7001 (+7.5%); Q3_K_S is 7.8638 (+26%); and Q2_K is 9.7516 (+56%) (llama.cpp documentation, 2026). A 2.8% perplexity rise hides a 5.5% RMS shift in the next-token distribution, an order of magnitude above Q6_K.
43	
44	The small-model story is contested. Precision-scaling laws fitted on 465 runs and validated to 1.7B parameters and 26B tokens find that post-training quantization loss increases as models are trained on more data, to the point that additional pretraining data can be "actively harmful" after quantization (Kumar et al., 2024). OmniQuant independently notes that 3–4 bit weight quantization can cause moderate-to-high losses, "especially for smaller models (1–10B)" (OmniQuant, 2024). Against this, a study of 350M–33B code models finds quantized models were more robust than full precision in 51.59% versus 42.86% of adversarial prompt experiments, and concludes that models below 3B handle aggressive quantization better than larger ones (Fang et al., 2025).
45	
46	On 8 GB, weights are not the binding constraint; the KV cache and the OS are. That makes "highest precision that fits" mostly right for 0.5B–1.5B, while 3B is forced to Q4 by the context budget. A 135M model should ship Q8_0 at roughly 0.14 GB because Q4 saves about 60 MB, less than a browser tab, while removing an already thin margin. A 0.5B should default to Q6_K at roughly 0.41 GB, with Q8_0 at roughly 0.53 GB when RAM allows and Q4_K_M only as an explicit low-memory toggle.
47	
48	| Model class | Default | Acceptable alternative | Avoid | KV | Rationale |
49	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
50	| 135M | Q8_0 (~0.14 GB) | Q6_K | ≤Q5_K_M | q8_0 | Q4 saves ~60 MB, less than a browser tab |
51	| 0.5B | Q6_K (~0.41 GB) | Q8_0 (~0.53 GB) | Q4_K_M except low-memory mode | q8_0 | Contested sensitivity; Q8 fits |
52	| 1.5B general | Q5_K_M (~1.07 GB) | Q4_K_M (~0.92 GB) | Q4_0, Q3, Q2 | q8_0 | Quality-per-byte sweet spot |
53	| 3B general | Q4_K_M (~1.83 GB) floor | Q5_K_M (~2.14 GB) at 4K | ≤Q3 | q8_0 | 8 GB plus context forces Q4 |
54	| 1.5B–3B code | Q5_K_M or Q6_K | Q4_K_M as floor | ≤Q4_0 | q8_0 | Format-sensitive; pass@1 drops are visible |
55	
56	KV quantization is the dominant memory lever at long context. Ollama describes q8_0 as "a very small loss in precision" and q4_0 as "a small-medium loss... more noticeable at higher context sizes" (Ollama, 2026). A GPU measurement on a 30B model at 128K found FP16 KV at 768 MiB, q8_0 at 408 MiB (−47%), and q4_0 at 216 MiB (−72%); prompt throughput was unchanged, but q4_0 generation fell 11.9% at 24K and **36.8% at 110K** (llama.cpp discussion #20969, 2026).
57	
58	## Small models are reliability-limited, not faculty-limited
59	
60	The sub-4B gains from 2024–2026 came mainly from over-training on filtered and synthetic data plus distillation from 7B–70B teachers, not from new architectures. SmolLM2-1.7B used roughly 11 trillion tokens in a multi-stage web, math, code, and instruction mix (Allal et al., 2025). A survey of 70 small models finds recent models typically use more than 1.5 trillion tokens, far above Chinchilla's roughly 20 tokens per parameter, and above about 1 trillion tokens data quality outweighs token count (Lu et al., 2025).
61	
62	The failure modes are compositional. Small models handle single-step transformations and local pattern matching, then collapse on multi-step reasoning, long-horizon tool use, factual recall, non-English tasks, and safety. Qwen2.5-1.5B scores 68.5 on GSM8K but 35.0 on MATH; Qwen2.5-0.5B scores 41.6 versus 19.5; Phi-3.5 scores 86.2 versus 48.5; Llama 3.2 3B scores 77.7 versus 48.0 (Qwen Team, 2024; Microsoft, 2024; Meta, 2024).
63	
64	The capability contract follows. A 135M model is for autocomplete, tone or format rewriting, keyword or field extraction, and classification — not chat, facts, arithmetic, code, or multi-turn memory. A 0.5B is for short replies, one-paragraph rewrites, summarising under 500 words, and flat key–value extraction — not facts, arithmetic, nested JSON, non-English, or more than two or three simultaneous constraints. A 1.5B is for paragraph drafting, email replies, short code with a code-tuned variant, single-turn RAG with citations, and one-level JSON — not multi-step math, tool calls, long context, or non-English nuance.
65	
66	Advertised context is an upper bound. RULER evaluated 17 long-context models on 13 tasks and found almost all degrade sharply with length; although all claimed at least 32K, only half maintained satisfactory performance at 32K (Hsieh et al., 2024). Llama 3.2 1B reports 96.8 exact match on single-needle NIAH but only 20.3 F1 on InfiniteBench En.QA, and Phi-3.5 Mini's RULER average falls from 94.3 at 4K to 63.6 at 128K, while Llama 3.1 8B retains 77.0 at 128K (Meta, 2024; Microsoft, 2024).
67	
68	The 2026 candidates are credible but vendor-reported. Qwen3.5-2B is Apache 2.0, 262K context, with thinking and non-thinking modes; its 2B is the quality sweet spot at MMLU-Pro 55.3/66.5, IFEval 61.2/78.6, and BFCL-V4 43.6, while the 0.8B is much weaker (Qwen Team, 2026). SmolLM3-3B is fully open weights, data, and recipe, 11.2 trillion tokens, 64K context, six languages, hybrid think/no-think, IFEval 76.7, and RULER-64K 67.9 (Hugging Face, 2025). Phi-4-mini is 3.8B, MIT-licensed, 5 trillion tokens, 128K context, MMLU 67.3, MMLU-Pro 52.8, GSM8K 88.6, and MATH 64.0 (Microsoft, 2025).
69	
70	## Evaluation is the product's only defensible source of truth
71	
72	The field's best practice converges on six controls: version and pin every pipeline element, disclose the prompt protocol verbatim, report more than accuracy, publish uncertainty, retain per-item outputs, and build in anti-contamination and anti-gaming mechanisms. HELM evaluated 30 models across 42 scenarios with seven metrics and released all raw prompts and completions; before HELM, models averaged coverage of only 17.9% of its core scenarios (Liang et al., 2023).
73	
74	Decontamination by exact match does not work because paraphrased items evade n-gram filters; refresh-based benchmarks such as LiveBench are a mitigation, and a metric can be reliable and still measure the wrong thing (Yang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; White et al., 2024; Jacobs & Wallach, 2021). The statistical problem is worse than most teams assume.
75	
76	Laptop measurement has a several-percent noise floor from the environment, not the model. Environment-only differences such as environment-block size and link order produced up to 8% performance change with identical source (Mytkowicz et al., 2009). Rigorous evaluation needs confidence intervals over independent repetitions and explicit separation of warm-up from steady state (Georges et al., 2007). `llama-bench` reports mean plus standard deviation and separates prompt processing from token generation, while its markdown table drops commit and variance; a published laptop methodology uses a trimmed mean of 15 runs (llama.cpp documentation, 2026; Mozilla.ai, 2025).
77	
78	A 20% speed threshold is roughly 7σ at CV = 3%, so it will miss the 8–15% regressions users notice, and the full config cross-product wastes hours on timing-only permutations while missing that flash-attention kernel selection perturbs numerics and mmap changes page-cache behavior. The three highest-leverage changes are per-item logging, splitting TTFT from TPOT at a 7% warning threshold, and recasting the quality fail as an absolute floor plus a confirmed large delta. Per-item logging unlocks every paired statistic for the cost of one file format; splitting the speed gate converts a blind threshold into a useful one; and the floor-plus-delta removes most flakiness while still catching breakage.
79	
80	| Element | Current state | Verdict | Change | Target |
81	|---|---|---|---|---|
82	| Suite size | 14 tasks, item counts unstated | Coverage strength, low power | Add a stratified 2,000-item subset across four domains | ≥2,000 items; ≥120 per task |
83	| Scoring | Point accuracy | Underpowered | Store per-item outcome: correct, parse-fail, schema-fail | 100% logged |
84	| Statistics | None stated | Major gap | Paired McNemar, Wilson CI, Holm, wild cluster bootstrap | α = 0.05; always report CI |
85	| `testHash` | SHA-256 of test content | Necessary, insufficient | `suiteFingerprint` over rendered prompts, answers, metric hash, few-shot pool, tokenizer hash, model hash, sampler, runtime commit | One hash, eight components |
86	| Baseline | Single versioned number | Insufficient | Seven runs: median, MAD, 95% CI, environment manifest; expires on OS, driver, or runtime change | ≥7 runs; 90-day expiry |
87	| Quality gate | Hard fail on any drop | Too sensitive | Floor at baseline − 5 pp, plus 5 pp delta at p < 0.001 confirmed on a second run | δ = 5 pp; p = 0.001 |
88	| Per-task gate | Per-task | Flaky | 15 pp warn; two consecutive runs fail; never fail on n < 120 | 15 pp, two runs |
89	| Parse failures | Untracked | Silent bias | First-class metric; +1 pp over baseline is T0 | ≤1% |
90	| Speed gate | Warn at 20% | Insensitive | Split TTFT and TPOT; warn 7%/10%, fail 20%/25% on two runs | Warn 7%; fail 20% |
91	| Repetitions | Unknown | Likely too few | One warm-up plus ten measured; median and MAD; CV ≤ 5% | 10 reps |
92	| Thermal | Unhandled | Confound | Three blocks; flag if block 3 exceeds block 1 by 5% | ≤5% drift |
93	| Config matrix | Full cross-product | Wasteful | Quality axes quant/KV/context; speed axes threads/batch/mmap; 200-item smoke | 200-item smoke |
94	| Contamination | None | Unaddressed | One private holdout; refresh 10% quarterly; canary string | One holdout |
95	| Comparability | Implicit | Fragile | Run manifest: hardware, OS, runtime commit, model hash, sampler, suite fingerprint | Manifest required |
96	
97	## Privacy is an engineering property, not a slogan
98	
99	Local-first software is about ownership of mutable user documents, not computation. Kleppmann and colleagues treat the local copy as primary and servers as secondary replicas; their seven ideals are no spinners, work not trapped on one device, network optional, seamless collaboration, the Long Now, security and privacy by default, and ultimate ownership (Kleppmann et al., 2019). The technical core is CRDTs for mergeable documents, notes, and editors, not model artifacts. The Long Now ideal assumes the last released software keeps running and formats stay readable; for AI, behavior also depends on tokenizer, chat template, quantization, runtime kernels, and hardware.
100	
101	The perception evidence is double-edged. In a controlled VR study with 60 participants, one group was told they were using cloud models and another local or on-premise models, while both were local; the "local" framing produced significantly higher UX and perceived response quality, and perceived data security rose significantly (p = .009, d = −0.52), while trust after interaction did not differ (VR framing study, 2026). A CHI EA 2026 on-device study found "conditional trust": participants reported epistemic uncertainty about data protection despite technically secure local deployment, and concluded that "invisible security measures are insufficient to foster trust" (CHI EA, 2026).
102	
103	The technical evidence says local inference is not a confidentiality boundary. "The Illusion of Local Privacy" tested model loading, runtime memory, wrapper persistence, and serving; a 24-hour AFL++ campaign with more than 12 million executions found no parser crashes or malformed GGUF loads, but recovered prompts from plaintext allocator memory, found wrappers persisting prompts in plaintext, found a llama.cpp flaw letting one authenticated client restore another's saved state in **200 out of 200 trials**, and found a prompt-prefix remote timing oracle (Ibrahim et al., 2026).
104	
105	Licensing is part of the trust story because weights are not code. The Llama 3.1 license grants use, reproduction, distribution, and modification, but distribution requires a copy of the agreement, a prominent "Built with Llama" notice, the specified notice text, and, for derivatives, "Llama" at the beginning of the model name; it has a 700 million monthly active user threshold and terminates on breach with a deletion requirement (Meta, 2024). Gemma redistribution requires the use restrictions as an enforceable provision, a copy of the agreement, prominent modification notices, and a notice file, and Google reserves the right to restrict usage remotely or otherwise (Google, 2026).
106	
107	The claim hierarchy is the copy deck. L0 is "inference runs on this computer," which almost every local tool can claim; L1 is "we operate no service that receives prompts," which most can claim; L2 is "no analytics, telemetry, or crash SDK," which many can claim; L3 is "normal use makes no network requests," which few can honestly claim because update checks and downloads violate it; L4 is "air-gapped mode verified," which is rare. ModelDuck should claim L0–L2, offer L3 through an Offline Mode that blocks catalog refresh, update checks, and telemetry, and claim L4 only after a tested air-gap mode.
108	
109	## Inference-time features: cheap wins, expensive traps
110	
111	RAG is the most credible usefulness upgrade, but direct evidence at 0.5B–3B is thinner than at 7B+. On CRAG, most advanced LLMs answered at most 34% correctly; straightforward RAG raised this only to 44%, and state-of-the-art industry RAG answered 63% without hallucination (Yang et al., 2024). Long context generally beat RAG on QA, while RAG was better for dialogue and general queries; across 20 LLMs, quality rose then fell as retrieved passages increased, with hard negatives a key cause (Li et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2024).
112	
113	Tool use is narrower than the demos suggest. On BFCL v4, `xLAM-2-1b-fc-r`, a 1B model fine-tuned for function calling, scores 30.44 overall, with agentic sub-scores in the low single digits (Patil et al., 2025). A 2025 BFCL-based edge study found 1–3B models significantly outperformed sub-1B models, reaching up to 65.74% overall and 55.62% multi-turn accuracy with hybrid SFT, PEFT, RL, and DPO optimization, while TinyAgent reports that a 1.1B model with curated function-calling data, tool retrieval, and quantization can achieve or surpass GPT-4-Turbo's function calling for a local Mac assistant, but that is an authors' claim on a narrow task (Haque et al., 2025; Erdogan et al., 2024).
114	
115	Prompt and KV caching are the best latency lever. Prompt Cache reports time-to-first-token improvements from 8× on GPU to **60× on CPU** for long, overlapping prompts, without changing outputs (Gim et al., 2024). llama.cpp supports prefix reuse and slot persistence: `cache_prompt` defaults true, `--cache-reuse N` controls minimum chunk reuse, and `/slots/{id}?action=save|restore` persists state, while node-llama-cpp exposes `saveStateToFile()` and `loadStateFromFile()` plus a custom `contextShift` strategy (llama.cpp discussion #13606, 2025; node-llama-cpp, 2026). The KV cache is the memory constraint: a Llama-3.2-3B-class model needs about 112 KiB per token in FP16, roughly 450 MB at 4K and 900 MB at 8K; q8_0 roughly halves this.
116	
117	Trust features are cheap and evidence-backed, but they can backfire. A human audit of four generative search engines found only **51.5% of generated sentences fully supported by citations** and only 74.5% of citations supporting their sentence, and on ELI5 even the best systems lacked complete citation support 50% of the time (Liu et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023). A roughly 12,000-query, seven-country experiment with a preregistered US sample found reference links and citations significantly increased trust in generative search **even when links or citations were incorrect or hallucinated**, while uncertainty highlighting reduced willingness to trust and share (Li & Aral, 2025).
118

143	## Claims ModelDuck should stop making or qualify
144	
145	The fastest quality improvement available is to stop making claims the evidence cannot support. Table 6 lists the claims most likely to appear in a local-LLM README, why each fails, and a defensible rewrite.
146	
147	| Claim | Why it fails | Defensible rewrite | Evidence |
148	|---|---|---|---|
149	| "Q4 is within 1–3% of FP16" or "Q4 is lossless" | No source defines the denominator; 8B Q4_K_M is +2.8% PPL, 5.5% RMS token-probability shift, ~1 pt MMLU; 3-bit GSM8K −9.3; 0.5B–3B GGUF task data absent | "On Llama-3.1-8B with llama.cpp b7600, Q4_K_M was within noise on HellaSwag, IFEval, and TruthfulQA, about 1 point lower on MMLU, and +0.24 PPL; at 0.5B–3B we report measured deltas per artifact." | T2: Kurt, 2026; T3: llama.cpp, 2026 |
150	| "Runs on 8 GB" without context, quant, KV, or browser state | 3B/8K is 6.2–7.2 GB before a browser; 32K is not viable; swap turns 15 tok/s into <1 | "3B Q4_K_M at 4K with q8 KV fits 8 GB with headroom; 8K is tight; 32K does not fit." | T1: Husom et al., 2025; T3: llama.cpp, 2026 |
151	| "128K context" or "long context" | Advertised window is an upper bound; RULER degrades; InfiniteBench 20.3 F1 at 96.8 needle; 3B/32K needs ~3.6 GB KV | "4–8K working context at 3B, 8–16K at 1.5B; use retrieval for more." | T1: Hsieh et al., 2024; T4: Meta, 2024 |
152	| "OpenAI-compatible" without a tested matrix | Tools, JSON schema, vision, streaming, and error shapes differ across local servers | "OpenAI-compatible chat/completions/models with streaming; tools, JSON, vision, and errors are covered by a published conformance matrix." | T3: LM Studio, 2026; T3: Ollama, 2026 |
153	| "No telemetry," "100% private," "your data never leaves your device" | Update checks, catalog refreshes, downloads, plaintext traces, localhost attacks, and LAN mode complicate the claim | "Inference is local; we operate no prompt service; no analytics or crash SDK. Network requests are limited to downloads you start, catalog refresh, and update checks; Offline Mode blocks all three." | T2/T6: Ibrahim et al., 2026; Local AI Scope, 2026 |
154	| "GPT-4-like" or "rivals 7B" | Vendor benchmarks are selected; cross-vendor numbers are incomparable; 3B is not an agent | State the capability contract: drafting, extraction, short code, grounded QA; not multi-step reasoning or autonomous tool use. | T4: Qwen Team, 2024; T4: Microsoft, 2024; T1: Lu et al., 2025 |
155	| "Reliable function calling" or "agents" | BFCL agentic scores are low single digits at 1B; τ-bench GPT-4o is <50% success; multi-step tool use is not reliable at 3B | "Single-turn tools with 3–5 functions, schema-validated arguments, and explicit confirmation; no autonomous multi-step loops." | T1: Patil et al., 2025; T2: Yao et al., 2024 |
156	| "Lossless Q8" | Q8_0 is within 0.04% PPL and ≤0.1 pt at 8B, not mathematically exact; small-model behavior unmeasured | "Q8_0 is F16-equivalent within measurement error at 8B on our suite." | T2: Kurt, 2026; T3: llama.cpp, 2026 |
157	| "Q4 is faster" | 41% faster in llama.cpp's reference bench, 2% on a 96-core Xeon; hardware and kernel dependent | "Q4 saves bytes; on this CPU we measure the actual speed difference and publish it." | T2: Kurt, 2026; T3: llama.cpp, 2026 |
158	| "Open source" for Llama or Gemma weights | Licenses restrict use, naming, redistribution, and termination; they are not OSI-open | "Open weights under the Llama/Gemma license; see the provenance card for terms." | T4: Meta, 2024; T4: Google, 2026 |
159	| "Local-first AI" | Local-first concerns ownership of mutable documents; inference behavior depends on runtime, quant, template, and hardware | "Local-first data: chats, attachments, settings, and model files are local and exportable; inference is local on this machine." | T1: Kleppmann et al., 2019 |
160	| "Energy efficient" without a meter | GreenBench's advantage is an M4 Pro preprint; x86 laptop energy is unmeasured; modelled energy is not measurement | Omit, or say "measured on this machine with a meter; boundary: package or system." | T2: GreenBench, 2026; T1: Husom et al., 2025 |
161	| "Deterministic benchmark" | Temperature 0 is not deterministic; batching, prefix caching, and chunked prefill move scores up to 15 pp | "Pinned, seeded, batch size 1; the noise floor is reported and the run manifest is published." | T2: Ouyang et al., 2025; T5: Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 |
162	| "Delete removes all traces" | WAL, backups, exports, swap, and SSD wear-leveling can retain copies; cryptographic erasure is not guaranteed | "Scoped delete with a documented residue map; no cryptographic-erasure promise." | T2: Murtuza, 2026 |
163	| "Enterprise-grade security" | No localhost-specific standard; local serving has cross-client state restore and timing-oracle flaws; auth is not tenant isolation | Publish the threat model and the tests: loopback binding, Host/Origin, token, CORS, LAN, tools, supply chain. | T2: Ibrahim et al., 2026; T3: OWASP REST, 2026 |
164	
165	## A 30/60/90-day roadmap for one maintainer
166	
167	The roadmap assumes one maintainer, a small Node codebase, and no new inference backend. It sequences evidence before features, because every later decision depends on the gate being trustworthy; each 30-day block has one primary workstream and two supporting ones.
168	
169	| Horizon | Workstream | Deliverable | Exit criterion |
170	|---|---|---|---|
171	| Days 0–30 | Evidence | Per-item logging, eight-component `suiteFingerprint`, run manifest, TTFT/TPOT split, 10 repetitions, thermal blocks | Ten A/A runs show false-alarm rate below 5%; baseline has at least seven runs and a 95% CI |
172	| Days 0–30 | Trust | Verify loopback binding, Host/Origin allowlist, per-install token, CORS off, JSON-only state changes, LAN opt-in | Cross-origin fetch, DNS rebinding, Host fuzzing, and cross-token state restore all fail |
173	| Days 0–30 | Product | Fit card, fail-closed 70–75% RAM policy, 4K/8K defaults, q8 KV | 3B/8K and 1.5B/8K measured on the target laptop; refusal works at threshold |
174	| Days 0–30 | Claims | Rewrite README, homepage, and API docs using Table 6; add evidence tags to model cards | Every public claim has a measured qualifier, an artifact hash, or a license link |
175	| Days 31–60 | Quality | Capability-floor quant policy; paired Q4/Q5/Q8 evaluation on 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B | CIs reported; no "1–3%" claim remains; per-model defaults updated |
176	| Days 31–60 | Retrieval | Hybrid BM25 plus dense retrieval, 22M reranker, extractive citations, abstention; grounded mode | Support rate and false-answer rate improve versus no-RAG; RSS stays within budget |
177	| Days 31–60 | Structure | Grammar-constrained final answer, semantic validation, one retry; TPOT measured | 100% schema validity; field accuracy reported; TPOT cost disclosed |
178	| Days 31–60 | Gate | Floor at baseline − 5 pp, confirmed 5 pp delta at p < 0.001, per-task 15 pp, parse-failure T0 | Gate catches a seeded regression and stays below 5% false alarms on A/A |
179	| Days 61–90 | Onboarding | Hardware scan, 2–3 recommendations, license, download, benchmark, first chat | Time-to-first-chat under 10 minutes on an 8 GB laptop |
180	| Days 61–90 | Provenance | Provenance card, license gate, SHA-256 pinning, export/import, scoped delete | Hash-mismatch and license-acceptance tests pass; export round-trips in CI |
181	| Days 61–90 | Privacy UX | Offline Mode, network ledger, API compatibility matrix and conformance tests | Zero unexpected egress in offline mode; chat, streaming, and error shapes pass |
182	| Days 61–90 | Catalog | Evaluate Qwen3.5-2B, SmolLM3-3B, Phi-4-mini on the same gate; test `ngram-mod` on code | Promotion only if >5 pp with CI; n-gram adopted only if ≥1.2× on code and no chat regression |
183	
184	## Methods, limitations, and unresolved contradictions
185	
186	This review synthesizes six research notes compiled on 30 October 2026: edge and CPU inference; GGUF quantization quality trade-offs; small-model capabilities; evaluation and benchmarking; inference-time features; and local-first product and security. The notes draw mainly on 2022–2026 sources, with older measurement and local-first work where relevant, and include peer-reviewed papers, preprints, official documentation, vendor claims, independent benchmarks, and practitioner reports. The search scope was deliberately narrow: local and edge inference of 0.5B–4B models, GGUF and post-training quantization, small-model capability and failure modes, evaluation methodology for single-machine deployments, privacy and security of local serving, and inference-time features that fit an 8 GB CPU laptop.
187	
188	Source quality is uneven. The strongest peer-reviewed evidence covers mechanisms (bandwidth-bound decode, KV quantization, attention), evaluation practice (HELM, BIG-bench, MLPerf, McNemar), small-model failure modes (RULER, GSM1k, MMLU-CF, FormatSpread), and local-first principles. The weakest evidence covers the exact product regime: no peer-reviewed study measures 0.5B–3B Q4 GGUF on an 8 GB Windows laptop; no peer-reviewed study measures CPU speculative decoding in that band; no study measures the KV-quantization decode penalty on CPU; and no independent benchmark covers the shortlist with identical prompts, templates, quantization, and CPU decoding. Several recent sources are preprints whose venues could not be verified, including GreenBench (2026), Kurt (2026), Kumar et al. (2024), Fang et al. (2025), Chavan (2026), SubTernary (2026), AdaptiveSD (2026), Speculative Illusion (2026), Ibrahim et al. (2026), Murtuza (2026), Weiss et al. (2026), and Zou (2026).
189	
190	The unresolved contradictions are substantive. On small-model quantization, Kumar and OmniQuant imply more caution below 1B, while Fang implies more robustness under adversarial prompts; the current judgment is that clean accuracy is likely more fragile and adversarial robustness can improve, which only a paired clean-and-adversarial evaluation at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B can settle. On Q4 speed, llama.cpp's 41% advantage and the Xeon's 2% difference are both real on their hardware, so no universal speed promise is possible without a per-CPU paired benchmark.
191	
192	## Conclusion
193	
194	The literature's most important finding for ModelDuck is not a model, a quant, or a feature. It is that the product's operating point is under-measured, and that the measurement apparatus is itself the differentiator. A local chat studio that can say "this artifact, on this laptop, at this context, lost 1.2 points on MMLU with a 95% interval, and here is the run manifest" has something no vendor benchmark can match. A studio that repeats "Q4 is lossless, 128K context, 100% private" has three claims it cannot defend and a support queue it cannot close.

## 2. Memory-budget fit card and fail-closed policy
**Recommendation:** Adopt now · **Rank:** 2 · **Evidence:** T1 mechanism + T6 measurements
**Problem.** “Runs on 8 GB” is not a property of a model; it is a property of a model,
quantization, context length, KV-cache type, runtime, and how much browser the user
has open. A 3B Q4 model at 8K is roughly 6.2–7.2 GB before the browser is counted.
When it crosses the line, the machine swaps and the user experiences a hang, not a
clean error.
**Proposal.** Before load, read the GGUF header and estimate: weights, KV cache at the
selected context and KV precision, runtime buffers, and an OS/browser reserve. Show a
three-state card — **Comfortable**, **Tight**, **Will not fit** — with the largest safe
context for that machine. Enforce the verdict at 70–75% of available RAM: refuse the
load with a specific remedy (“reduce context to 4K,” “use q8 KV,” “close the browser”)
rather than allowing swap.
Expose the same estimate in the model picker and in the API error path. Record the
actual peak RSS after load and compare it with the estimate so the estimator can be
calibrated over time.
**Evidence.** The review’s arithmetic puts 3B/8K at 6.2–7.2 GB before a browser,
while 1.5B/8K and 3B/4K sit in a safer range. KV cache, not weight bits, is the
binding constraint at long context: a Llama-3.2-3B-class model needs about 112 KiB
per token in FP16, roughly 0.9 GB at 8K and 3.6 GB at 32K. q8_0 KV roughly halves
that with near-free quality loss; symmetric q4_0 KV is a quality cliff.
**Smallest credible experiment.** On the target 8 GB laptop, load 3B/8K, 3B/4K, and
1.5B/8K. Record peak RSS, swap, time-to-first-token, and tokens per second. Verify
that the 70–75% refusal triggers before the OS swaps.
**Pass gate.** No configuration that passes the card swaps or drops below 5 tokens
per second; every refusal names a concrete remedy; the estimate is within 15% of
measured peak RSS.
**Cost and risk.** Low to medium. The estimator needs model-architecture metadata and
a small amount of calibration. Be conservative: a false “comfortable” verdict is much
worse than a false “tight” verdict.
---
## 3. Prompt/KV cache with cache-aware ordering
**Recommendation:** Adopt now · **Rank:** 3 · **Evidence:** T1 + T3 + T6
**Problem.** Multi-turn chat re-prefills the same system prompt, retrieved context,
and conversation prefix on every turn. On CPU that can turn a short reply into a
minute of prefill, especially at 4K–8K context. The user perceives the model as slow
even when decode speed is fine.
**Proposal.** Keep a stable prefix: system prompt, tool/schema instructions, and
long-lived retrieved context first; volatile turns last. Reuse the KV cache for the
unchanged prefix, expose cache-hit tokens and TTFT in the UI, and persist a
conversation checkpoint so reopening a chat does not re-prefill from zero.
Use llama.cpp’s prefix reuse and slot persistence (`cache_prompt`, `--cache-reuse`,
`/slots/{id}?action=save|restore`) or node-llama-cpp’s `saveStateToFile()` /
`loadStateFromFile()`. Choose a context-shift policy deliberately: shifting the
window destroys the cache, so summarize or truncate at a turn boundary instead of
silently shifting mid-conversation.
**Evidence.** Prompt Cache reports 8× TTFT improvement on GPU and up to 60× on CPU
for long overlapping prompts without changing outputs (Gim et al., 2024). llama.cpp
can reuse a 43-token prefix as one cached block. The review’s own tests show context
shift is the enemy of cache reuse.
**Smallest credible experiment.** Run a 20-turn scripted chat with cache on and off.
Measure TTFT, cache-hit tokens, peak RSS, and answer quality on the same prompts.
**Pass gate.** Median TTFT drops by at least 2× after the first turn; cache-hit tokens
are visible; no answer changes on a fixed-seed comparison; RSS stays within the
memory card’s budget.
**Cost and risk.** Low. The main risk is stale cache after a settings change; version
the cache key by model hash, sampler, and prefix hash.
---
## 4. Loopback security baseline and LAN opt-in
**Recommendation:** Adopt now · **Rank:** 4 · **Evidence:** T5/T6 + T3
**Problem.** “Bound to 127.0.0.1” is not a security boundary. A malicious website can
attempt cross-origin requests, DNS rebinding can reach localhost, and a local server
that trusts any `Origin` or stores state per client can leak one client’s data to
another. Local tools have already shipped CORS `*` defaults and cross-client state
restore bugs.
**Proposal.** Enforce a small, testable baseline:
- bind to `127.0.0.1` by default; require an explicit LAN opt-in and a warning;
- validate `Host` against an allowlist and reject unexpected `Origin` values;
- require a per-install bearer token for `/v1/*` when authentication is enabled;
- keep CORS off by default; allow only explicit origins;
- accept JSON content types for state-changing routes and reject simple-form CSRF;
- isolate saved slots/state by token, not just by slot id;
- put LAN mode behind TLS and a separate threat-model page.
**Evidence.** The review documents “0.0.0.0 Day,” an Ollama CVE, llama.cpp CORS `*`,
and a llama.cpp flaw that let one authenticated client restore another client’s saved
state in 200 of 200 trials (Ibrahim et al., 2026). OWASP’s REST guidance supports
explicit origin checks, token auth, and content-type enforcement.
**Smallest credible experiment.** Run four negative tests: cross-origin `fetch`,
DNS-rebinding host header, Host-header fuzzing, and cross-token state restore. All
must fail closed. Then run the same tests with LAN mode explicitly enabled and verify
the warning and TLS requirements.
**Pass gate.** All four attacks fail; the server logs the rejected origin/host; no
state is readable across tokens; the LAN opt-in cannot be enabled accidentally.
**Cost and risk.** Low. The main risk is breaking legitimate local integrations;
provide a documented token and a clear error message.
---
## 5. Claim hierarchy, Offline Mode, and a network ledger
**Recommendation:** Adopt now · **Rank:** 5 · **Evidence:** T1/T2/T6
**Problem.** “No telemetry” and “your data never leaves your device” are not the same
claim, and neither is automatically true. Update checks, catalog refreshes, model
downloads, crash reporters, and browser requests can all create egress. Users cannot
verify a claim they cannot see.
**Proposal.** Adopt a five-level claim hierarchy (L0–L4):
- **L0:** inference runs on this computer;
- **L1:** we operate no service that receives prompts;
- **L2:** no analytics, telemetry, or crash SDK;
- **L3:** normal use makes no network requests;
- **L4:** air-gapped mode is verified.

input.content:
# Analysis of the research reports

**Date:** 2026-10-30
**Scope:** the four files in `reports/` and the six research notes in
`research_notes/ModelDuck local LLM literature review/` (about 350 KB in total).
**Method:**
- I read every report section.
- I checked each factual claim about ModelDuck or Research Engine against the code at HEAD
  (`modelduck` 1c9876d plus today's uncommitted fixes; `research-engine` 6533434 plus another agent's
  uncommitted work).
- I fetched four load-bearing sources to check that they exist and say what is quoted.
- I mapped every recommendation to the idea register.

## Verdict in one paragraph

The reports are sound on direction and mostly accurate on facts. Their one systematic weakness is
that they reason from the literature and from the code's *shape*, so they miss defects that only
show up when the code runs. On 30 October, running probes found four ModelDuck defects:
- the CORS and authentication bypass (IDEA-1054);
- a crash or hang on a malformed GGUF header (IDEA-967);
- a model file corrupted by a double download (IDEA-882);
- lost chats past 200 (IDEA-1047).

None of the reports names any of them. On the GGUF crash, the literature review's evidence points
the wrong way. Where the register disagrees with the reports, it is mainly because I deferred the
review's "adopt now" measurement work using generic reasons. Two of those deferrals should be revised
(see "Register actions").

## 1. ModelDuck local LLM literature review and the six notes

**What it is.** A synthesis of six notes, with evidence tags from T1 (peer-reviewed) to T6
(practitioner reports). It argues that ModelDuck's operating point is unmeasured and that its
measurement apparatus is the differentiator. It produces 15 ranked ideas: 8 adopt, 4 prototype,
1 defer and 2 reject.

**Source quality (spot-checked).**

| Source | Exists | Supports the claim | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ibrahim et al. 2026, arXiv:2609.18526 | yes | yes: 12M-exec AFL++ found no parser crashes; 200/200 slot-restore flaw; prefix-timing oracle | The paper does not name the fuzzed parser. The 200/200 flaw is llama.cpp `--slot-save-path` authorisation, not GGUF parsing |
| llama.cpp perplexity README | yes | yes: F16 6.2332, Q8_0 6.2343, Q4_K_M 6.4071, RMS Δp 5.52 %, Q4_0 6.7001 | Llama **3** 8B on an RTX 4090. The note labels it correctly; one line in the quantization note blends it with Kurt's Llama-**3.1**-8B task scores |
| llama.cpp discussion #23470 | yes | partly | A user experiment, not a maintainer benchmark. "Cliff" is the review's word. The q4_0-KV damage depends on the model: 375/500 answers changed on Qwen2.5-7B, 2/500 on a 27B |
| Kurt 2026, arXiv:2601.14277 | yes | yes | All 16 uses cite the quantization study correctly |

Overall, the citations are real and quoted accurately. The review's own limitation section flags
the preprints it could not verify, which is honest.

**Claims about ModelDuck, checked against the code.**

| Review claim | Code today | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Quality gate: hard fail on any drop | `benchmarks/run.mjs:679`: fails on a quality delta below −0.01 pts | **True** |
| Speed gate warns at 20 % | `run.mjs:676` | **True** |
| 14 tasks, item counts unstated | 14 prompts; the README's percentages are out of 21 checks (95.2 % = 20/21) | **True**, and the sample is smaller than implied |
| No per-item logging or paired statistics | No McNemar, Wilson or Holm anywhere in `benchmarks/` | **True** |
| `testHash` misses prompt and runtime | Fixed by the generation manifest (07f0c4d) | **Stale** |
| Defaults: 4K context, q8 KV; reject 32K | Default 4096; Balanced preset q8_0; maximum 32768, not a default | **Already compliant** |
| q4_0 KV is a cliff | ModelDuck's own run: Qwen2.5-0.5B with Q4 KV scored 19.1 % vs 85.7 %; the Token saver preset still uses q4_0 (`src/config.js:61`) | **True for the shipped 0.5B; the preset is still exposed** |
| Ship a 135M model at Q8_0 and a 0.5B at Q6_K | The catalog ships both at Q4_K_M; its own data shows 0.5B Q8 at 95.2 % vs Q4 at 85.7 % | **Not adopted.** The 2-item gap is suggestive, not significant, at n = 21 |
| "No telemetry" needs an egress ledger | README line 6: "Everything stays on your computer." `getLlama()` is called without `build`, so node-llama-cpp defaults to `"auto"` and may download and build llama.cpp from source | **Real gap.** Undisclosed egress is possible; not reproduced |
| Cross-client state restore and timing oracle | Each `/v1` request gets a fresh session that is dropped afterwards (`src/openai.js:144,334,373`) | **Does not apply** to ModelDuck |
| "Deterministic benchmark" is an overclaim | README line 99 says "deterministic"; the benchmark seeds 42 at batch 1 but publishes no noise floor | **Partly true:** reword or report the noise floor |

**Reasoning flaw.** Brief 1 says "fourteen independent tests at α = 0.05 give a 51 % false-alarm
risk". That figure belongs to a significance-tested gate. ModelDuck's gate is a deterministic
threshold, so its real problem is different: any single flipped check fails the run, and a pass
proves little at n = 21. The recommendation, per-item logging plus a floor and a confirmed delta,
is still right.

**Blind spot.** The review cites Ibrahim et al.'s result, "no parser crashes or malformed GGUF
loads", as reassurance. ModelDuck parses headers with node-llama-cpp's JavaScript
`readGgufFileInfo`, and a 100-byte header made it run out of memory or hang (IDEA-967). Fuzzing
evidence about one parser does not transfer to another; the probe was what settled it.

## 2. ModelDuck idea briefs

These are faithful expansions of the review's 15 rows, each with a smallest experiment and a pass
gate. Status against the code:

| Brief | Register | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Per-item logging and paired statistics | 1037 Deferred | Not built. **Should be Approved** (rank 1; the gate weakness is confirmed) |
| 2 Memory-fit card, fail-closed | 903 Approved (narrowed) | Engine silently retries smaller contexts. **Widen 903** to the estimate-and-refuse design |
| 3 Prompt/KV cache | 873 Deferred | Sessions are reused per chat (a56065e); the default `contextOverflow: "shift"` discards the cache, as the brief warns |
| 4 Loopback security baseline | 1054 Integrating | Built today. Cross-origin, rebinding and CORS-default cases are tested. Open: LAN TLS, logging refused origins |
| 5 Claim hierarchy, Offline Mode, egress ledger | 1039 Deferred | README overclaims slightly; `build: "auto"` egress is undisclosed. **New idea needed** (see below) |
| 6 Extractive citations | 1040 Deferred | No retrieval exists, so deferring is correct |
| 7 Grammar plus semantic validation | 859 / 1041 Deferred | Grammar exists (`engine #grammarFor`); semantic validation does not |
| 8 Capability-floor quantization | 907 / 1044 Deferred | The catalog contradicts it (above). The Token saver preset is the concrete risk |
| 9–11 Retrieval, memory, n-gram | 870 / 1042 / 1043 Deferred | Prototype ideas; deferring matches "prototype with a kill criterion" |
| 12 Evaluate Qwen3.5-2B, SmolLM3-3B, Phi-4-mini | not registered | An evaluation task, not a code idea; run it once brief 1 is in place |
| 13–15 Draft speculation, 32K, agents | 904 Deferred / compliant / rejected | Consistent with the briefs |

## 3. ModelDuck — what to borrow from NeuroCore

This report is accurate about both codebases at the time it was written, and right to reject
porting NeuroCore's architecture.

| Idea | Register | Status today |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Generation manifest | 1000 Rejected (implemented) | Done by 07f0c4d; the manifest also records history truncation |
| 2 Versioned presets with benchmark-gated trust | 1001 Deferred | **README line 135 claims presets "only earn trust after both phases pass", but nothing records trust.** Fix the wording, or build idea 2 |
| 3 Pre-flight load plan | 903 / 1002 | Same as brief 2 |
| 4 Per-request and JIT budget | 1003 Deferred | Confirmed: no wall-time cap and no JIT load limit. Low urgency now that LAN and CORS require auth |
| 5 Latency monitor; 8 Trend report | 1004 / 1017 Deferred | Not built; additive |
| 6 Untrusted fence | 1015 Rejected | No tools or retrieval yet; becomes a prerequisite if MCP lands |
| 7 SSRF-safe acquisition | 1016 Deferred | Still curated-catalog only; IDEA-862 (hash) is the near-term part |
| 9 Destructive-route confirmation | 1018 Rejected | The UI confirms, and the routes are same-origin since ADR-018 |

**Blind spot.** Its security row says "partial; add the missing pieces", but none of its ideas
covers the LAN/CORS authentication bypass found on 30 October.

## 4. Research Engine — cross-project mechanic mining

This is a careful report. It correctly put the in-flight T-015 task ahead of everything else.

**Current-state claim:** the README is over its 22,500-character test limit. **Still true:** the
working copy is 22,567 bytes, with another agent's task at Phase 4.

**Tiers against the register:**
- Tier 1: 974 and 975 Approved; 971, 972, 973 and 976 Deferred.
- Tier 2 and 3: the anchored ledger, coverage-aware consensus and code registry were Approved as
  981, 978 and 984.

**Why it diverges:** I approved the items that close a verified integrity gap (retraction bypass,
unverified digest, unbound kill-test, unbound cascade preview). I deferred the report's
feature-shaped Tier 1 items: analysis records, meta-analysis, bibliography import and snapshot
semantics. That is defensible. However, 971 (immutable analysis records with re-analysis) is
closer to an integrity gap than I credited, so revisit it after T-015.

## Register actions this analysis supports

1. **IDEA-1037 → Approved, P2.** The gate weakness is confirmed in code; it is the review's rank 1.
2. **IDEA-903 → widen** to brief 2: estimate memory, show Comfortable / Tight / Will not fit, and
   refuse with a remedy.
3. **New, P2:** pass `build: "never"` (or an explicit opt-in) to `getLlama()` so loading a model
   cannot silently download and compile llama.cpp. Disclose network use in the README.
4. **New, P3:** move the Token saver preset from q4_0 to q8_0 KV, gated on a benchmark run;
   consider Q8_0 or Q6_K defaults for the 135M and 0.5B catalog entries.
5. **New, P4 (docs):** qualify README line 6 ("Everything stays on your computer") and line 99
   ("deterministic"), and fix the preset-trust claim on line 135.
6. **Research Engine 971:** re-review after T-015 completes.

## Housekeeping

`reports/` and `research_notes/` are untracked in AIKit's repository; commit them so the research
and this analysis are not lost.

content.text:
I've analyzed all four reports and the six research notes, and written the results to [reports/Report analysis 2026-10-30.md](reports/Report%20analysis%202026-10-30.md). The register is unchanged until you decide on the six actions below.

**How reliable they are:** they hold up well on direction and facts. I checked four sources the review leans on: all exist and are quoted accurately. Two of the review's points about them needed correcting:
- **The fuzzing paper doesn't name the parser it tested.**
- **The "q4_0 KV cliff" comes from one user's experiment,** and the effect varies a lot by model. ModelDuck's own run (19.1% at Q4 KV, against 85.7% normally) shows it does apply to its 0.5B model.

**Their weak spot:** they reason from literature and the code's structure rather than running it. None of the four defects that today's probes found shows up in the reports (website access, the bad-file crash, double-download corruption, lost chats). On the crash, the review cites a fuzzing study that found "no parser crashes" as reassurance. That study tested a different parser from the JavaScript one ModelDuck uses, which crashed on a 100-byte file.

**The reports' factual claims about ModelDuck, checked against the code:**
- **Confirmed:**
  - the benchmark fails on any drop of more than 0.01 points;
  - it has only 21 checks and no per-item statistics;
  - the speed warning triggers at 20%;
  - the Token saver preset still uses the 4-bit KV setting;
  - the catalog ships Q4 for the 135M and 0.5B models, against both the review and ModelDuck's own Q8 result.
- **Out of date:** the prompt-fingerprint gap was closed by commit `07f0c4d`.
- **Doesn't apply:** the cross-client cache leak, because each API request gets its own session.

**New problems the analysis turned up:**
- **Possible silent downloads.** ModelDuck lets node-llama-cpp download and compile llama.cpp when no prebuilt binary fits, while the README says "Everything stays on your computer." This comes from the library's documented default; I haven't triggered it.
- **An unsupported README claim.** It says presets "only earn trust after both phases pass", but nothing records that.
- **Research-engine still fails its own test.** Its README is still over the 22,500-character limit, as the research-engine report warned.

**Where my verdicts and the reports disagree:** I deferred the review's top-ranked measurement work (1037) with a generic reason, and narrowed the memory-fit idea (903). For research-engine, I approved verified integrity gaps over the report's feature-style tier 1 items, which I think is defensible. 971 (immutable analysis records) deserves a second look once that project's active task finishes.

**Register changes the analysis supports:**
1. **1037: approve as P2.** It's the review's #1, and the code confirms the gate is a raw threshold.
2. **903: widen it** to estimate memory, show whether the model fits, and refuse with a fix when it doesn't.
3. **New, P2:** set `build: "never"` in ModelDuck so loading a model can never silently download and compile llama.cpp.
4. **New, P3:** move the Token saver preset to 8-bit KV, after a benchmark run, and reconsider the 135M and 0.5B default quantizations.
5. **New, P4 (docs):** qualify three README claims: "Everything stays on your computer", "deterministic", and presets "earning trust".
6. **Research-engine 971:** re-review once its active task completes.

Should I apply these six register changes? Separately, I'd also recommend committing `reports/` and `research_notes/`, which are still untracked.

# Dossier: Evidence-Grade Measurement, Trust and Small-Model Features (ModelDuck)

- **Source URL**: `reports/ModelDuck local LLM literature review.md` (local synthesis, 2026-10-30)
- **Source License**: `Local research report; cited papers and specifications retain their own licenses`
- **Analyzed Commit / Date**: `working tree` / `2026-10-30`
- **Primary Stack**: Node.js 20+ ESM, standard-library HTTP server, vanilla HTML/CSS/JS UI, `node-llama-cpp` CPU GGUF inference, OpenAI-compatible chat API.

## 1. Executive Summary & Core Architecture

The 2026 ModelDuck review reaches a narrow conclusion: the product's exact operating point - 0.5B-3B Q4 GGUF, one user, batch 1, an 8 GB Windows CPU laptop - is almost unmeasured in the literature. The rigorous systems work is at 7B and above on GPUs, where throughput is batching-limited; the edge work uses different hardware and power budgets. What transfers is physics and method: decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, quality belongs to a specific quantization artifact and prompt path, small models fail compositionally, and small unpaired benchmarks cannot detect the effects that matter.

Most of the review's fifteen ranked ideas already have register entries: `IDEA-873`/`905`/`940`/`954` cover prompt and KV caching; `IDEA-903`/`1002` cover memory-fit preflight and blocking load plans; `IDEA-924`/`968` cover loopback protection; `IDEA-884` covers offline mode; `IDEA-907` covers quantization policy; `IDEA-870`/`998` cover retrieval and reranking; `IDEA-939` covers conversation summarization; `IDEA-904`/`953` cover draft-model speculation; `IDEA-923`/`954` cover context limits; and `IDEA-860`/`871`/`1015` cover tools and agents. This dossier therefore extracts only the ideas that are not already represented, or whose mechanism is materially different from the existing entry.

Three gaps remain. First, the benchmark gate records per-prompt results but reduces them to point estimates, so it has low statistical power and cannot separate a model regression from parser or prompt drift. Second, privacy and grounding claims have no evidence surface: there is no network ledger, no claim ladder, no citation-support check, and no semantic validation for schema-valid but wrong output. Third, several evidence-backed small-model features are missing: editable fact-table memory, n-gram self-speculation (blocked on runtime support), and a benchmark-gated model-promotion path.

### Coverage map: the review's fifteen ideas

| Review idea | Register coverage |
|---|---|
| 1. Per-item logging, `suiteFingerprint`, paired statistics | `IDEA-1037` (new), with `IDEA-1038` (new run manifest); extends `IDEA-1000` and `IDEA-1017` |
| 2. Memory-budget fit card and fail-closed policy | `IDEA-903`, `IDEA-1002` |
| 3. Prompt/KV cache with cache-aware ordering | `IDEA-873`, `IDEA-905`, `IDEA-940`, `IDEA-954` |
| 4. Loopback security baseline and LAN opt-in | `IDEA-924`, `IDEA-968` |
| 5. Claim hierarchy, Offline Mode, network ledger | `IDEA-1039` (new); extends `IDEA-884` |
| 6. Extractive citations, abstention, verification UI | `IDEA-1040` (new); composes with `IDEA-870` and `IDEA-998` |

# Dossier: Report Analysis Follow-ups (ModelDuck)

- **Source URL**: `reports/Report analysis 2026-10-30.md` (private local analysis of the four research reports)
- **Source License**: `Local analysis; cited papers and specifications retain their own licenses`
- **Analyzed Commit / Date**: `modelduck 1c9876d + uncommitted ADR-018..020` / `2026-10-30`
- **Primary Stack**: Node.js 20+ ESM, `node-llama-cpp` 3.22.2, vanilla UI.

## 1. Executive Summary & Core Architecture

Checking the literature review's claims against ModelDuck's code confirmed three gaps that no register entry covered. First, `getLlama()` is called without a `build` option, so node-llama-cpp's default (`"auto"`) may download and compile llama.cpp when no prebuilt binary fits; the README promises "Everything stays on your computer." Second, the Token saver preset still uses q4_0 KV, which ModelDuck's own baseline measured at 19.1 % against 85.7 %. Third, three README claims overstate what the code guarantees.

## 2. Target Routing Matrix

> The routing below records the first analysis. `../ideas.json` and the generated `../MATRIX.md` are authoritative for the current target and decision status.

| Idea ID | Concept Name | Target Project | Value Score (1-5) | Complexity (Low/Med/High) | Recommended Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `IDEA-NEXT-1` | No Silent Runtime Build or Download | `modelduck` | 4 | Low | Adopt |
| `IDEA-NEXT-2` | Token Saver Preset on q8_0 KV | `modelduck` | 3 | Low | Adopt after benchmark |
| `IDEA-NEXT-3` | Evidence-Scoped README Claims | `modelduck` | 3 | Low | Adopt |

---

## 3. Extracted Ideas & Cold-Start Implementation Blueprints

### No Silent Runtime Build or Download
- **Target Project**: `modelduck`
- **Source**: `src/engine.js:181,197` (`getLlama` without `build`); node-llama-cpp `getLlama.d.ts` (`build` defaults to `"auto"`)
- **Priority / Effort vs. Impact**: High Impact / Low Effort

#### Core Mechanism & Value
Pass `build: "never"` so the runtime uses only the installed prebuilt binaries. A missing binary becomes an actionable error instead of a hidden GitHub download and a long compile.

#### Potential Improvements
Makes the "no network except downloads you start" claim true; removes a multi-minute hang on unusual CPUs.

#### Potential Weaknesses
A machine without a matching prebuilt binary can no longer load models automatically.

#### How to Combat These
Map the failure to a Why/Fix error that names `npx node-llama-cpp source download` as an explicit, user-started step; keep the existing GPU-to-CPU fallback.

#### Cold-Start Agent Implementation Blueprint
1. Add `build: "never"` to both `getLlama` calls in `src/engine.js`.
2. Map a binary-not-found failure to an AppError with Why/Fix.
3. Document network use in the README.

### Token Saver Preset on q8_0 KV
- **Target Project**: `modelduck`
- **Source**: `src/config.js:61`; README benchmark table (Q4 KV 19.1 % vs 85.7 %)
- **Priority / Effort vs. Impact**: Medium Impact / Low Effort

#### Core Mechanism & Value
Swap the preset's KV cache from q4_0 to q8_0, which the baseline shows is close to F16, keeping the small context and batch that save memory.

#### Potential Improvements
The lightest preset stops destroying quality on the 0.5B model.

#### Potential Weaknesses
Uses more KV memory than q4_0 (about 2× the q4 KV size).

#### How to Combat These
Run both benchmark phases and update the README table before shipping (generation changes are benchmark-gated).

#### Cold-Start Agent Implementation Blueprint
1. Change `kvCache` to `q8_0` in `token_saver`; update its description.
2. Run `npm run bench:model` and `npm run bench:chat`; record the run.

### Evidence-Scoped README Claims
- **Target Project**: `modelduck`
- **Source**: `README.md:6` ("Everything stays on your computer"), `:99` ("deterministic"), `:135` (presets "only earn trust after both phases pass")
- **Priority / Effort vs. Impact**: Medium Impact / Low Effort

#### Core Mechanism & Value
State what is measured or enforced: chats and prompts stay local, network use is limited to downloads the user starts; the benchmark is seeded at batch 1 with single runs; presets are benchmark-first but trust is not recorded.

#### Potential Improvements
Removes claims the review's Table 6 flags as indefensible.

#### Potential Weaknesses
Plainer copy reads less impressive.

#### How to Combat These
Keep each claim with its evidence, which is the product's stated differentiator.

#### Cold-Start Agent Implementation Blueprint
1. Rewrite the three sentences; keep the README under its size budget.

input.command:
cat >> .aikit/decisions.md <<'EOF'

### ADR-021: No on-demand runtime build, stalled-download watchdog, pre-load memory fit
- **Date**: 2026-10-30
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The analysis of the research reports (IDEA-1061, 1063, 853, 903) found four gaps:
  - `getLlama()` was called without `build`, so node-llama-cpp's default `"auto"` could download and compile llama.cpp when no prebuilt binary fits. The README promised that "everything stays on your computer".
  - A download that stopped sending data stayed "downloading" forever and held one of the two slots.
  - A load that did not fit either pushed the machine into swap or silently retried smaller contexts.
  - Three README sentences claimed more than the code enforces.
- **Decision**:
  - Both `getLlama` calls pass `build: "never"`. A missing binary becomes `runtime_binary_missing`, whose fix names the explicit `npx node-llama-cpp source download` step. The runtime loader is injectable for tests.
  - `DownloadManager` aborts a job after `idleTimeoutMs` (60 s) without data and reports it as **stalled**, keeping the `.part` file for resume.
  - `src/memory-fit.js` estimates weights + KV (2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes per element × context) + a 256 MiB reserve. The KV shape comes from GGUF metadata, which the registry now records as `kvShape`.
  - The engine compares the estimate with free RAM plus the currently loaded model. Above 75 % it refuses with `507 model_will_not_fit` and the largest context that fits. `force` (the UI's **Load anyway**) overrides the refusal. GPU offload and unknown shapes are never refused.
  - The loaded state carries `fit` and `contextFallback` ({requested, actual, reason}), and the UI raises a toast for a reduced context or a tight fit.
  - The README now scopes its network, benchmark and preset-trust claims.
- **Consequences**:
  - A real Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4 model loads with `build: "never"` from the installed prebuilt binary, and its metadata yields the expected 28 KiB per token of F16 KV.
  - The estimate is not yet calibrated against measured peak RSS (brief 2's ±15 % gate). With mmap, part of the weights is evictable, which is why the user can override the refusal.
  - The refusal now covers the case where Windows `os.freemem()` is low and the machine would swap.
EOF
cd ../.. && python aikit.py check modelduck 2>&1 | grep -E "FAIL|gates passed"

result.output:
# ModelDuck benchmark

ModelDuck has two benchmark gates. They answer two different questions:

1. **Model reload phase** — which model file and loading configuration should we
   use? It varies model family, quantization, KV cache type, context length,
   batch size, CPU threads, thread pool, sequences, flash attention, mmap, GPU
   layers and context checkpoints.
2. **Model usage phase** — once a model configuration is fixed, which sampling
   and prompting setup gives the best answers? It varies temperature, top-k,
   top-p, min-p, repeat penalty, repeated user prompts, reasoning directives,
   system prompts and JSON-schema structured output.

```bash
npm run bench:model -- --download   # first run: fetch missing models
npm run bench:chat
npm run bench:update                # deliberately replace both baselines
npm run bench:report
npm run bench:link                  # after commit: run once per pending phase
```

The suite runs through the same `LlamaEngine` the UI uses. It starts with
SmolLM2 135M, Qwen2.5 0.5B and Qwen2.5 Coder 1.5B, and adds Qwen2.5 1.5B,
Llama 3.2 3B and Phi-3.5 Mini plus Q4/Q5/Q8 variants for the reload phase.
The fourteen tasks cover exact instruction following, arithmetic, factual
recall, reasoning, multiple-choice HellaSwag/MMLU-style questions, a GSM8K-style
word problem, JSON shape, JavaScript parsing, lowercase formatting, list
cardinality, reading comprehension, long-context recall and bug repair.

Quality is the percentage of deterministic checks passed. Speed is the median
generated tokens per second. `runtimeMs` is the whole variant's wall-clock time.
The model phase runs one-factor-at-a-time on representative models; the chat
phase runs generation-only variants on the model configuration chosen by the
first phase. Temperature is 0 for the model phase and 42-seed sampling for the
chat phase.

## Test identity

`benchmarks/suite.mjs` exports `SUITE_VERSION`. Every result also carries a
SHA-256 `testHash` over the prompts, checks, global and per-variant system
prompts, `promptIds` and effective matrix defaults. A baseline with a different
hash is not comparable: the runner refuses to claim a quality change until the
test changelog is reviewed and the baseline is deliberately updated. A different
node-llama-cpp version or manifest version is refused the same way.
See [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

Every model result records its GGUF chat-template hash, and every prompt result
stores the generation manifest digest, prompt digest and truncated-history
digest. That makes a result traceable to the exact system prompt, history,
template and sampling settings the model saw, independently from the test hash.
A baseline with a different model file size or chat-template hash is refused
before the run starts; `--update-baseline` is the deliberate override.

## Unsupported by node-llama-cpp 3.22.2

These are recorded in every result's `capabilities.unsupported` field:

- physical batch size (`n_ubatch` is not exposed separately from `batchSize`)
- unified KV cache (`kv_unified` is not exposed)
- RoPE frequency base and scale

ROCm is not a node-llama-cpp backend. AMD GPUs use Vulkan; NVIDIA uses CUDA;
Apple uses Metal. A backend build may require the vendor toolchain.

## History database

Every run writes:

- `benchmarks/history.jsonl` — tracked, append-only run/link events and the
  durable record that can rebuild the database.
- `benchmarks/history.sqlite` — ignored local DB with `runs`, `model_results`,
  `prompt_results` and `commits` tables; `phase`, `test_hash` and every variant
  setting are queryable.

A run made before its commit is pending. `npm run bench:link` attaches it to the
new HEAD; `npm run bench:report` shows quality, speed, runtime and the
`v<suite>:<hash>` identity per commit. Node 22+ is required for `node:sqlite`;
the app itself remains Node 20+. The app's **Bench** button reads the two
baseline files and this JSONL history to show the same per-test percentages,
runtime and linked commit without a terminal.
  501 benchmarks/history.mjs
   99 benchmarks/link.mjs
  316 benchmarks/matrix.mjs
  243 benchmarks/report.mjs
  713 benchmarks/run.mjs
  312 benchmarks/suite.mjs
   75 benchmarks/test-hash.mjs
  250 benchmarks/verify-manifest.mjs
 2509 total
latest.json

The test definitions are versioned separately from the application and from the
model settings. Every run records `suiteVersion` and a SHA-256 `testHash` of the
prompts, checks and matrix entries. If those definitions change, the hash changes
and the baseline must be updated deliberately; a result delta is then visibly a
test change, not a model/settings regression.

| Version | Date | Change |
|---|---|---|
| v1 | 2026-10-30 | Initial 9 tasks: exact word, arithmetic, factual, reasoning, JSON, JavaScript, lowercase, list, needle. |
| v2 | 2026-10-30 | Added HellaSwag-style choice, MMLU-style choice, GSM8K-style word problem, reading comprehension and bug-fix tasks. |
| v3 | 2026-10-30 | Split into model-reload and chat-usage phases; added quantization, KV cache, context/batch/thread/sequence/flash/mmap/checkpoint variants and sampling/system/reasoning/prompt-repeat/structured-output variants. |
| v4 | 2026-10-30 | Hash the global and per-variant system prompts, `promptIds`, effective sampling defaults and the generation-manifest version. Every run also records node-llama-cpp/Node versions, model chat-template hashes and a per-generation manifest digest; a runtime, model-file size or chat-template mismatch is refused like a test-hash mismatch. |

When adding or changing a prompt, check or matrix variant:

1. Bump `SUITE_VERSION` in `benchmarks/suite.mjs`.
